entities.summary:
The February Revolution was a pivotal event in modern world history, marking the beginning of the end of the Russian monarchy and the rise of the Soviet Union. On February 23, 1917, a wave of protests and strikes swept through the streets of Saint Petersburg, as workers, soldiers, and intellectuals demanded an end to the war with Germany and the overthrow of the Romanov dynasty. The revolution was sparked by a combination of factors, including the catastrophic conditions of World War I, the economic hardship and poverty that had plagued Russia for decades, and the growing discontent among the population with the autocratic rule of Tsar Nicholas II. 

 The revolution was led by a coalition of socialist and liberal parties, including the Mensheviks and the Socialist Revolutionary Party, who had been secretly planning the uprising for months. On February 27, a provisional government was formed, with Alexander Kerensky as its leader. However, the revolution was not without its challenges, as the provisional government struggled to maintain order and stability in the face of growing opposition from the Tsarist forces and the rising power of the Bolsheviks. 

 The February Revolution had far-reaching consequences, leading to the eventual collapse of the Romanov dynasty and the establishment of the Soviet Union. It also paved the way for the rise of Vladimir Lenin and the Bolsheviks, who would go on to shape the course of Russian and world history for decades to come. 

 As Lenin himself later noted, 'The February Revolution marked the beginning of a new era, in which the working class would take power and establish a socialist society.'
